summary:
Annuality and perenniality are flexible plant life-history strategies that shape evolution and agriculture. Annuals complete their life cycle in one year; perennials live for more than two. Annuality has evolved independently across many plant families, and either habit may be ancestral. The balance often depends on survival and reproduction: annuals tend to fare better where adult mortality is high and conditions fluctuate, while perennials benefit where adults survive well. Shifts also involve trade-offs in reproductive investment and are linked to traits such as mating system, seed dormancy, and vegetative regrowth.

Perennials often reproduce repeatedly and can persist through clonal growth, while annuals reproduce once and may survive between seasons as dormant seeds. These patterns have exceptions and can vary within species.

Agriculture has favored annual crops, but perennial crops can reduce erosion, conserve water and nutrients, store more carbon, and resist pests. Developing productive perennial grains remains challenging because of trade-offs and long juvenile periods.
